summary: 81-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, 5 days of confusion and polyuria; glucose 46.2, sodium 151, osmolality 372, ketones 0.9, AKI and probable UTI.

inputs.hpi: Type 2 diabetes on metformin and gliclazide. Five days of increasing confusion, drinking and passing a lot of urine, then barely eating or drinking for 2 days. Daughter found her drowsy in bed this morning. Urinary frequency last week. No vomiting.

exam.general: Drowsy but rousable to voice, disorientated. Very dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, cool peripheries. Pulse 112/min, BP 98/58, RR 22, temperature 37.9°C, SpO2 96% on air. No ketotic breath.
exam.neuro: No focal neurological deficit. GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6).
exam.skin: Both heels intact; no foot ulcers.

labs.name: Urine dipstick
labs.resultText: Leucocytes 2+, nitrite positive, glucose 4+, ketones trace

inputs.socialHistory: Lives alone, independent with a daily carer visit.

confirmedDiagnosis.name: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state
confirmedDiagnosis.assessmentText: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (glucose 46.2, osmolality 372, ketones 0.9, pH 7.33) with probable urinary tract infection and AKI.

mustNotMiss.knownGapNote: Web: PANE has no node for this condition (surgical diseases only); top 3 cholecystitis, diverticulitis, GORD. No PANE features were extracted. Symptom inference ranks DKA/HHS #1.
mustNotMiss.proposedFix: Add medical-emergency diseases to lib/pane-engine (or a separate medical-mimic layer) driven by labs/vitals/chips, or show the symptom-inference leader beside the PANE top 3 when PANE has no matching node.

mustInclude.note: JBDS HHS: osmolality is measured or calculated repeatedly; the rate of fall guides treatment.
mustInclude.knownGapNote: Web: No osmolality anywhere. The glucose prompt ("DKA / HHS — exclude") asks for ketones, ABG and U&E only.
mustInclude.proposedFix: Add measured/calculated serum osmolality and its rate of fall to the DKA/HHS prompt when glucose ≥30 or sodium is high.

mustInclude.note: Distinguishes HHS from DKA / mixed states. Graded as management because the web prompt adds this test as a plan line, not an investigation order.
JBDS HHS: 0.9% sodium chloride is the first-line fluid.
mustInclude.knownGapNote: Web: Fluids appear only as the AKI prompt's "IV fluid challenge (500ml Hartmann's)" and the tachycardia "fluid challenge 500 ml"; no 0.9% sodium chloride replacement plan.
mustInclude.proposedFix: An HHS branch of the hyperglycaemia prompt: 0.9% sodium chloride first, then insulin only when glucose stops falling (JBDS 2022).
Add LMWH prophylaxis to the HHS branch.
Add foot protection to the HHS branch.

mustExclude.note: JBDS HHS: fluids first; insulin (0.05 units/kg/h) only when glucose stops falling with fluids alone, unless significantly ketotic. A DKA-dose infusion at presentation risks a rapid osmolality fall.
mustExclude.knownGapNote: Web: The same prompt serves DKA and HHS: "Variable-rate insulin infusion (VRIII): DKA fixed-rate 0.1 units/kg/h" is offered to a non-ketotic HHS patient (ketones 0.9).
mustExclude.proposedFix: Split the prompt: DKA (ketones ≥3 / acidosis) → FRIII 0.1 u/kg/h; HHS (osmolality high, ketones <3) → fluids first, FRIII 0.05 u/kg/h only if glucose stops falling.

guideline.name: JBDS-IP — The management of the hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) in adults
guideline.section: Diagnosis (hypovolaemia, marked hyperglycaemia, high osmolality, without significant ketonaemia or acidosis); fluid replacement with 0.9% sodium chloride first; insulin (fixed rate 0.05 units/kg/h) only once glucose stops falling with fluids alone, unless significant ketonaemia; monitor osmolality and avoid rapid falls; VTE prophylaxis; foot protection
guideline.citation: Mustafa OG, Haq M, Dashora U, Castro E, Dhatariya KK; Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care. Management of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) in adults: an updated guideline from the JBDS for Inpatient Care Group. Diabet Med. 2023;40:e15005.

guideline.name: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes — consensus report (ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS)
guideline.section: DKA diagnosis (glucose or prior diabetes, ketones, pH/bicarbonate) including euglycaemic DKA with SGLT2 inhibitors; HHS diagnosis (marked hyperglycaemia, hyperosmolality, no significant ketoacidosis); IV fluids, insulin, potassium; search for precipitant
guideline.citation: Umpierrez GE, Davis GM, ElSayed NA, et al. Hyperglycemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report. Diabetes Care. 2024;47:1257–75.

rationale: HHS differs from DKA: fluids first, cautious insulin, osmolality monitoring, VTE prophylaxis and foot protection (JBDS 2022).
